question: My lessor just texted me that my rent in Kangaroo Point, QLD is going up $60 per week starting next month. They already increased it 7 months ago. There's no letter, no form — just a message on my phone. I'm a student and can barely afford this place as it is. Do I have to pay the increase?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: Whether a text message constitutes a valid rent increase notice under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD), and whether the minimum period between increases has been complied with.

RULE: Under section 93 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD), a lessor must not increase the rent at intervals of less than 12 months from the date of the last increase. Further, the lessor must give the tenant at least 2 months' written notice of the proposed increase. The notice must be in the approved form, which requires it to be in writing and specify the amount of the increase and the date it takes effect. Under section 92, if the tenant believes the rent increase is excessive, the tenant may apply to QCAT for an order to reduce the rent or set aside the increase.

APPLICATION: The lessor sent a text message — not the approved written form. Only one month's notice was provided, far less than the 2-month minimum. The last rent increase was only 7 months ago, which is less than the statutory 12-month interval. The increase is presumptively invalid on all three grounds.

CONCLUSION: The rent increase is invalid under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) because: the notice was not in the approved written form, inadequate notice was given (only 1 month instead of 2), and the 12-month interval under section 93 was not respected. The tenant should inform the lessor in writing that the increase is invalid and continue paying the current rent. If the lessor insists, the tenant may apply to QCAT under section 92 to dispute the increase.

question: My rent in South Brisbane went from $400 to $550 a week — that's a 37.5% increase! The lessor gave proper written notice and 2 months' warning, so the paperwork is fine, but the amount feels predatory. Similar apartments in West End are renting for $400-430. Is there anything I can do about the amount?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: Whether a tenant can challenge a rent increase as excessive even when the lessor has complied with the procedural requirements under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Section 92 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) provides that a tenant who receives a notice of a rent increase may apply to QCAT for an order to reduce the rent increase or set it aside if the tenant considers it excessive. QCAT may consider factors including: the range of market rents for comparable premises in the locality, the proposed increased rent compared to the current rent, the state of repair of the premises, the term of the tenancy, the period since the last rent increase, and any other matter QCAT considers relevant. The application must be made within 30 days of receiving the notice.

APPLICATION: The increase of 37.5% ($400 to $550) significantly exceeds the market range for comparable apartments in West End ($400-$430). While the lessor's notice was procedurally compliant, the quantum of the increase is disproportionate to market rates and appears to be significantly above the general market level for comparable premises.

CONCLUSION: The tenant may apply to QCAT under section 92 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) within 30 days of receiving the notice to have the rent increase reduced or set aside as excessive. The tenant should gather evidence of comparable rental listings in South Brisbane and West End, document the condition of the premises, and reference the unusually large percentage increase. QCAT may order the increase be reduced to a more reasonable level or disallowed entirely.

question: I'm 9 days behind on rent for the very first time in my 2 years at West End, QLD. My employer accidentally underpaid me this month and it'll be fixed next week. The lessor just put a 'Notice to Leave' in my letterbox saying I have 7 days to get out. I can pay the arrears on Friday when my corrected pay comes through. Will I be evicted?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: Whether a notice to leave for rent arrears requires a minimum notice period and whether paying the arrears remedies the breach under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD), a lessor may give a notice to leave for non-payment of rent where the tenant is at least 7 days in arrears. Section 326 sets out the requirements for a notice to leave: it must be in the approved form, state the ground for termination, and give the tenant a minimum of 7 days to leave. However, for the first occasion of non-payment of rent in a 12-month period, if the tenant pays the outstanding rent within the notice period, the notice ceases to have effect. Section 277 provides that a residential tenancy agreement ends only in accordance with the Act. The lessor cannot self-help evict — they must apply to QCAT for a termination order if the tenant does not vacate.

APPLICATION: The tenant is 9 days in arrears for the first time in 2 years. The notice gives 7 days but must be in the approved form. If the tenant pays the outstanding rent before the notice expires, the notice ceases to have effect (first occasion provision).

CONCLUSION: The notice to leave must be in the approved form and give at least 7 days under section 326 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD). If the tenant pays the arrears within the notice period (the first occasion of non-payment in 12 months), the notice is of no effect and the tenancy continues. The tenant should pay immediately on Friday and keep proof of payment. A lessor cannot physically remove a tenant without a QCAT termination order.

question: I signed a 12-month lease in Fortitude Valley, QLD 5 months ago but I need to move to Sydney for a new job next month. I know I'm breaking the lease early. What notice do I need to give the lessor and what costs could I be liable for?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: What notice period a tenant must give and what compensation they may be liable for when breaking a fixed-term residential tenancy agreement early under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Under section 327 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD), a tenant who wishes to end a fixed-term agreement early must give a notice of intention to leave in the approved form. For a general tenant-initiated termination (where no breach by the lessor is alleged), the notice must give at least 2 weeks' notice. However, breaking a fixed-term agreement constitutes a breach, and the lessor is entitled to claim reasonable compensation for losses suffered as a result of the early termination. This may include: reasonable re-letting costs (advertising, agent fees), and loss of rent for the period the premises remain vacant until a new tenant is found. The lessor has a duty to mitigate their loss by taking reasonable steps to re-let the premises promptly. Section 277 outlines how agreements end. Any claim for compensation must be reasonable and proportionate.

APPLICATION: The tenant is 5 months into a 12-month lease and needs to relocate for work. The tenant must give at least 2 weeks' written notice in the approved form. The lessor must make reasonable efforts to re-let.

CONCLUSION: The tenant must give at least 2 weeks' written notice in the approved form under section 327 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD). The lessor may claim reasonable re-letting costs (e.g. advertising fees) and rent for any vacancy period, but must take reasonable steps to minimise the loss by finding a new tenant promptly. The tenant should continue paying rent until a new tenant commences. If the lessor demands an unreasonable amount, the tenant may apply to QCAT.

question: I've lived in the same apartment in Toowong, QLD for 6 years, always paid rent on time, no issues. The lessor just gave me a notice to leave saying they want to renovate and then move their family in. It says I have 2 months. This feels like they just want to re-let at a higher rent — can I challenge this at QCAT?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: Whether a tenant can challenge a notice to leave given on grounds of renovation or lessor occupancy under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD), a lessor may give a notice to leave without grounds (at the end of a periodic agreement with 2 months' notice), or on specific grounds such as the lessor requiring the premises for their own residence or for major renovations requiring vacant possession. Under section 286 and related provisions, a notice to leave must be in the approved form, specify the ground for termination, and provide the required notice period (generally 2 months for a 'without grounds' notice or lessor occupancy). If a tenant believes the notice is retaliatory or the stated ground is not genuine, the tenant may apply to QCAT to challenge the notice. QCAT (formerly the 'tribunal') has the power to set aside a notice to leave if it is satisfied it was given in retaliation for the tenant enforcing their rights, or that the ground stated is not genuine.

APPLICATION: The tenant has a 6-year exemplary tenancy history. The notice states renovation and family occupancy. The tenant suspects the real motivation is to re-let at a higher rent. The tenant may apply to QCAT to challenge the genuineness of the stated ground.

CONCLUSION: The tenant may apply to QCAT under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) to challenge the notice to leave. The tenant should gather evidence: their rental payment history, any recent requests for repairs (which might suggest retaliation), comparable rental listings at higher rents, and any communications with the lessor. If QCAT finds the stated ground is not genuine or the notice is retaliatory, it may set the notice aside. The tenant should file the application promptly — before the notice expiry date.

question: My air conditioner completely broke 3 days ago in my rental in Indooroopilly, QLD, and it's 34 degrees. I've called the lessor's agent 4 times and left messages — no call back. My elderly mother lives with me and is struggling in the heat. Can I get it fixed myself and claim the cost from the lessor?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: Whether a tenant can arrange urgent repairs and recover the cost from the lessor when the lessor or agent fails to respond under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Section 185 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) requires the lessor to maintain the premises in good repair and ensure the premises are fit for the tenant to live in. The lessor must also ensure that the premises and inclusions are in a reasonable state of cleanliness and repair at the start of the tenancy. Where an urgent repair is required, the tenant may arrange for a qualified person to carry out the repair up to the value prescribed (currently 2 weeks' rent) if: (a) the tenant has taken reasonable steps to contact the lessor or their nominated repairer, and (b) the lessor or nominated repairer has not responded within a reasonable time. The lessor must reimburse the tenant for the reasonable cost of the repair. Section 191 provides for QCAT orders in relation to repairs. In QLD's climate, a broken air conditioner during summer, particularly affecting a vulnerable occupant, constitutes an urgent repair.

APPLICATION: The air conditioner has been broken for 3 days in 34-degree heat. The tenant has called 4 times without response. An elderly occupant is affected. The tenant has satisfied the requirement to make reasonable contact attempts. The repair cost cap (2 weeks' rent) should be sufficient for a standard air conditioning repair.

CONCLUSION: The tenant may arrange the repair and recover the cost from the lessor under section 185 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD). The tenant should: continue documenting all contact attempts, use a qualified tradesperson, obtain a detailed receipt, and provide it to the lessor with a written request for reimbursement within 7 days. If the lessor refuses to reimburse, the tenant may apply to QCAT under section 191 for an order requiring payment.

question: The bathroom ceiling in my rental in Chermside, QLD has been leaking every time it rains for 2 months now. I've sent the lessor 3 written emails with photos. They replied once saying 'we'll look into it' but nothing has happened. Mold is now growing and the ceiling looks like it might collapse. What can I legally do to force action?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: What remedies are available to a tenant when the lessor fails to carry out non-urgent repairs after repeated notification under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Section 185 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) imposes a duty on the lessor to maintain the premises in good repair and fit for habitation. A leaking ceiling that is causing mold growth and structural deterioration is a breach of this obligation. Under section 191, if the lessor fails to comply with their obligation to repair within a reasonable time after being notified, the tenant may apply to QCAT for orders including: requiring the lessor to carry out the repairs, reducing the rent until the repairs are completed, or terminating the tenancy. Section 94 provides for rent decreases where the premises are partially uninhabitable or services are reduced. The tenant may apply for a rent reduction for the period during which the premises have been affected by the unrepaired leak.

APPLICATION: The tenant has sent 3 written emails with photos over a 2-month period, far exceeding a reasonable notification period. The ceiling is deteriorating and mold is growing. The premises may be partly unfit for habitation. This is well beyond the stage where the lessor has had a reasonable opportunity to respond.

CONCLUSION: The tenant may apply to QCAT under section 191 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) for orders requiring the lessor to carry out the repairs. The tenant should present: copies of all emails and photos, a record of any verbal communications, the date the leak was first reported, and photographs of the current condition. The tenant may also seek a rent reduction under section 94 for the period the premises have been affected. If the ceiling presents an imminent risk of collapse, the tenant should mention this as an urgent safety concern.

question: A hidden water pipe in the wall of my rental in Spring Hill, QLD burst over the weekend and flooded the lounge room carpet. The lessor says I have to pay for the carpet replacement because the damage happened while I was living there. The plumber that came out said the pipe was corroded from age and would have burst regardless of who lived there. Who's responsible?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: Whether a tenant is liable for damage caused by a structural failure (aged and corroded water pipe) under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Section 185 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) imposes a duty on the lessor to maintain the premises in good repair, which includes the plumbing and structural elements of the premises. A burst water pipe caused by age and corrosion is a structural failure within the lessor's responsibility. The tenant is only liable for damage they cause through their own act, neglect, or default. Section 188 provides that a tenant must keep the premises clean and must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises. Where damage is caused by a latent defect, structural failure, or ordinary deterioration — not by any act or omission of the tenant — the lessor bears the cost of repair.

APPLICATION: The plumber confirmed the pipe burst due to age-related corrosion, not any act by the tenant. The damage to the carpet is a direct consequence of the structural failure. The tenant bears no liability for damage caused by ordinary deterioration of the premises' fixtures.

CONCLUSION: The tenant is not liable for the carpet replacement cost. Under sections 185 and 188 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD), the lessor is responsible for maintaining the plumbing and repairing damage caused by structural failures that are not the tenant's fault. The tenant should provide the lessor with the plumber's report confirming the cause was age-related corrosion. If the lessor insists on payment or attempts to deduct this from the bond, the tenant should dispute the claim through the RTA's bond dispute process and apply to QCAT if necessary.

question: I'm moving out of my rental in Milton, QLD in 2 weeks. The lessor is already threatening to keep my bond for scuff marks and a small chip in the kitchen bench. The agent never gave me an entry condition report when I moved in 18 months ago — I asked for one but they never provided it. Can they still claim against my bond?
ground_truth:
ISSUE: Whether a lessor can make a claim against a rental bond for alleged damage when no entry condition report was provided to the tenant under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD), a lessor must complete an entry condition report and give a copy to the tenant at the start of the tenancy. The condition report is the primary evidence of the state of the premises at commencement. Section 112 defines the maximum rental bond that may be required. Sections 124 and 127 address bond payments and joint applications for bond refunds. Without a completed entry condition report signed by both parties, the lessor has no evidentiary basis to establish that the alleged damage occurred during the tenancy. The Residential Tenancies Authority (RTA) administers the bond dispute process. If the tenant disputes the lessor's claim, the bond is held until the parties resolve the dispute or QCAT makes an order.

APPLICATION: The lessor never provided an entry condition report despite the tenant's request. The scuff marks and chip in the kitchen bench cannot be proven to have occurred during the tenancy without a condition report as a baseline. The lessor has no evidence of the premises' condition at the start of the tenancy.

CONCLUSION: The lessor has no valid evidentiary basis to claim against the bond. Under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD), the lessor's failure to complete an entry condition report is a breach of their obligations. The tenant should submit a Refund of Rental Bond (Form 4) to the RTA. If the lessor disputes the refund, the RTA will hold the disputed amount and the parties may apply to QCAT. The tenant should present evidence that no entry condition report was provided. The lessor's failure to comply with the condition report requirements significantly weakens any bond claim.

question: The lessor is asking for a bond of $2,600 for a $650-per-week apartment in New Farm, QLD. That works out to 4 weeks' rent. I've heard the maximum bond in QLD is 4 weeks — is it different for furnished vs unfurnished places? Just want to make sure I'm not being overcharged.
ground_truth:
ISSUE: Whether a lessor can lawfully demand a rental bond of 4 weeks' rent under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD).

RULE: Section 112 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) defines the maximum rental bond that may be required for a residential tenancy agreement. Where the weekly rent is $700 or less, the maximum bond is 4 weeks' rent. Where the weekly rent exceeds $700, there is no statutory maximum specified in the Act for the bond, though the bond must still be reasonable. Section 111 defines what constitutes a rental bond. The bond must be lodged with the RTA within 10 days of receipt by the lessor. Unlike some other states, QLD does not have a separate higher bond threshold for furnished premises.

APPLICATION: The weekly rent is $650, which is under the $700 threshold. Four weeks' rent at $650/week = $2,600. This is at the statutory maximum, not in excess. The amount is lawful.

CONCLUSION: The bond of $2,600 (4 weeks' rent at $650/week) is at the maximum permitted under section 112 of the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (QLD) and is lawful. The tenant should ensure the bond is lodged with the RTA within 10 days and obtain a receipt confirming lodgment. The tenant should also request a copy of the entry condition report at the start of the tenancy.
